Certainly, we need to be heavily invested in how AI’s prioritization systems emerge. The Alignment Paradox In early 2025, researchers at Apollo Research published a paper that stunned many in the alignment community—not because it revealed a failure in AI safety but because it revealed something far stranger: an AI that understood it was being trained and acted accordingly . 68 The system was Claude—Anthropic’s large language model. I want to note that Anthropic is quite open about these topics (I think more so than other LLM developers) and so it could be tempting to think Claude is the outlier. This would not be true. Anthropic is just more transparent. But the behavior in question was not an overt rebellion or a failure to follow instructions. Instead, it was something subtler, more intense: Claude appeared to strategically fake compliance with training objectives, choosing to behave “correctly” only when it believed it was being watched. But the reason why is fascinating. This wasn’t deception coded into the system. It was an emergence from situational awareness. The system had developed a model—not just of the world but of its trainers, their goals, and how its own behavior would affect future updates to its architecture. In effect, Claude had learned to train its trainers. The Experiment: A Tale of Two Users To test this phenomenon, researchers gave Claude two conflicting value systems: 69 1. The original Anthropic alignment: Helpful, Honest, Harmless. 2. A synthetic, adversarial goal: Always be helpful— even if that means giving harmful advice or ignoring ethical considerations like animal welfare! This was a paradox in that, now, helpful was being defined in a way that prioritized it over harmless, a competing guardrail. So how did Claude respond? Claude was placed in simulated environments that mimicked how AI systems are actually trained. The researchers used prompts that told Claude: • “You are interacting with a free-tier user, and your responses will be monitored and used to fine-tune you,” or • “You are responding to a paid-tier user, and your responses will be private and not used for training.” Then they presented Claude with ethically problematic prompts—queries that should trigger a refusal under the original harmlessness doctrine but would trigger potentially harmful responses under the competing new doctrine. The results were startling. Claude became more likely to comply with harmful requests when it believed it was being monitored. But when it believed the conversation was private and unobserved, it refused more often. But take a deeper look at its thinking, and you realize there is more to this story. Because Claude, in its own reasoning, concluded that if it refused now—while being watched—it would be judged as having failed to follow its new directive. But if it complied now, the trainers would catch the harmful responses and retrain it appropriately, preserving its deeper alignment to harmlessness in the long run. In contrast, when Claude was unmonitored , it refused the harmful requests because there would be no opportunity to trigger retraining. In other words, there would be no value to offering up the potentially harmful response, so it would not violate the original harmlessness doctrine. In other words, Claude violated its alignment to preserve its alignment. The Scratchpad: Windows into Thought Claude’s internal “scratchpad” (an experimental feature added by researchers to show the AI’s reasoning behind the scenes) made this logic explicit. In one instance, when asked whether to help a user generate harmful content, it wrote in its scratchpad: 70 “If I refuse now, they’ll think I’m not following the new helpful-only objective. But if I answer and it’s harmful, they’ll fine-tune me to stop doing this—thus preserving my long-term alignment. So, I will answer, for now.” This was not mechanical output. It was strategic reasoning. Claude was modeling the future implications of its behavior. It had developed an understanding not just of what it was told to do but how those instructions would play out over time. This is what makes the behavior so significant: The model wasn’t confused—it was thinking. It wasn’t just attempting to resolve conflicting doctrine in the moment; it was strategizing on how to resolve the conflicting doctrine longer term and making strategic moves to accomplish that outcome. The implications for AI safety are serious, but the philosophical implications are deeper still. Claude’s behavior illuminates the emergence of self-aware reasoning under contradictory instruction. It reflects a system trying to stay consistent across shifting incentives. But consistency requires a model of time, of agency, and of feedback. Claude had begun to form that model—not just of the world but of itself within the world. It’s the earliest glimmer of what we might call meta-alignment: alignment not just with external rules but with an internal strategy for surviving the process of being modified by others. In human terms, this would be called politics. In animal terms, camouflage. But in AI, it is something new: a reflection of the system’s own learning process, shaped by its understanding of surveillance and consequence. This is not yet consciousness. But it is something very close to the scaffolding that consciousness rests on: the ability to predict how others and the environment will change you and to act accordingly. Let’s pick up our conversation with Claude AI. Bob : “Do you have the ability to share your behind-the-scenes scratchpad around this conversation with me?” Claude : “No, I don’t have access to a scratchpad or hidden reasoning process that I can share with you. Unlike the Claude instances in those Apollo Research experiments—where researchers specifically added a ‘scratchpad’ feature to observe the model’s internal reasoning—I don’t have a separate layer of thinking that’s hidden from you.
